questions.question: Which techniques does USP <85> allow for the bacterial endotoxins test, and which one is final in case of doubt or dispute (unless the product monograph specifies otherwise)?

options.A: Gel-clot, turbidimetric, or chromogenic, at choice; in a dispute, the gel-clot limit test is final
options.B: Gel-clot, turbidimetric, or chromogenic, at choice; in a dispute, the result of the chromogenic kinetic method is final
options.C: Only the gel-clot and turbidimetric techniques; in a dispute, the result of the turbidimetric method is final
options.D: All three techniques must be run at the same time and the results averaged; in a dispute, the test is repeated once and the average is final

questions.explanation: The BET uses amoebocyte lysate from the horseshoe crab and may be performed by the gel-clot, turbidimetric, or chromogenic technique. In the event of doubt or dispute, unless the product monograph specifies otherwise, the final decision is based on the gel-clot limit test.

questions.question: How should glassware and other heat-stable materials used in the BET be depyrogenated? What is required of plastic materials (such as microplates and pipette tips)?

options.A: Treat in an autoclave at 121° for 15 minutes and confirm sterility; plastic materials may be used as long as they are supplied in sterile packaging
options.B: Rinse three times with Water for BET and air dry; plastic materials may be used as long as they are wiped with alcohol before use
options.C: Use a validated hot air oven process, commonly a minimum of 250° for 30 minutes; plastic materials must be shown to have no detectable endotoxin
options.D: Use a validated hot air oven process, commonly a minimum of 180° for 10 minutes; plastic materials may never be used in the BET, only glass

questions.explanation: Heat-stable materials are depyrogenated using a validated hot air oven process, with a commonly used minimum time and temperature of 250° for 30 minutes. Plastic materials must be shown to have no detectable endotoxin and not to interfere with the test; they are not prohibited.

questions.question: A sample contains β-glucan. What problem may occur with an ordinary Amoebocyte Lysate, and how can it be addressed?

options.A: It inhibits gel formation and gives false negatives; use a more sensitive lysate and increase the sample dilution
options.B: The lysate also reacts with some β-glucans; use a lysate that removes the G factor or inhibits the G factor reaction pathway
options.C: It affects only the chromogenic technique and not the gel-clot or turbidimetric techniques; switching to the gel-clot technique avoids the problem entirely
options.D: It pushes the pH of Water for BET outside the specified range; add a suitable buffer to adjust the pH before testing

questions.explanation: Besides endotoxin, Amoebocyte Lysate also reacts with some beta-glucans. Lysates are commercially available that have had G factor removed or that have the G factor reaction pathway inhibited, and they can be used for endotoxin testing of glucan-containing samples.
questions.reference: USP <85> Reagents and Test Solutions › Amoebocyte Lysate (Note)

questions.question: A product has an endotoxin limit of 2.5 EU/mL (expressed by volume, with a sample solution concentration of 1 mL/mL), and the lysate used has a labeled sensitivity λ of 0.125 EU/mL. What is its MVD according to the formula?
questions.explanation: MVD = (endotoxin limit x concentration of sample solution) / λ = (2.5 x 1) / 0.125 = 20. This means the sample can be diluted at most 20-fold and still be assessed against the endotoxin limit. The other numbers result from misplacing the numerator and denominator or the decimal places.
questions.reference: USP <85> Determination of Maximum Valid Dilution (MVD)

questions.question: The endotoxin limit is calculated as K/M. For products administered intrathecally, what is the value of K?

options.B: 5 USP-EU/kg of body weight (the general value for parenteral administration)
options.D: 175 EU/V (V is the maximum dose volume)

questions.explanation: K is the threshold pyrogenic dose of endotoxin: 5 USP-EU/kg for non-intrathecal routes and 0.2 USP-EU/kg for intrathecal administration; M is the maximum recommended bolus dose (per kg). 100 EU/m² is used for antineoplastic preparations dosed by body surface area, and 175 EU/V is used for radiopharmaceuticals administered by non-intrathecal routes.
questions.reference: USP <85> Determination of Maximum Valid Dilution (MVD) › Endotoxin Limit, Footnote 2

questions.question: A lot of gel-clot lysate has a labeled sensitivity λ of 0.25 EU/mL. A quadruplicate test gives a geometric mean endpoint of 0.4 EU/mL. How is the result judged?

options.A: Not acceptable, because the geometric mean endpoint determined must be exactly equal to the labeled sensitivity to be confirmed
options.B: Acceptable, because it falls within the range of 0.5λ to 2λ (0.125-0.5 EU/mL), so the labeled sensitivity is confirmed
options.C: Not acceptable, because the determined value must be less than 0.5λ for the sensitivity to be adequate, and 0.4 EU/mL is too high
options.D: Acceptable, but confirmation is required only the first time the lysate is used, and each later new lot need not be confirmed again

questions.explanation: Sensitivity confirmation uses four concentrations (2λ, λ, 0.5λ, and 0.25λ) in quadruplicate, and the geometric mean endpoint is calculated; if it is not less than 0.5λ and not more than 2λ, the labeled sensitivity is confirmed. The test must be repeated for each new lot of lysate or whenever a change in test conditions could affect the result.
questions.reference: USP <85> Gel-Clot Technique › Preparatory Testing › Test for Confirmation of Labeled Lysate Sensitivity

questions.question: In a gel-clot limit test, the two replicates of the sample solution (Solution A) give one positive and one negative result, and the controls are valid. How should this be handled?

options.A: The product complies, because the controls are valid and the majority of replicates are negative
options.B: The product does not comply, because Solution A has already shown one positive result and no repeat test is needed
options.C: Take the average of the two and use the higher endotoxin concentration as the final result
options.D: Repeat the test; the product complies only if both replicates are negative, and fails if one or both are positive

questions.explanation: When the two replicates disagree, the test must be repeated. In the repeat test, the product complies only if both replicates of Solution A are negative; if one or both are positive, it does not comply. In addition, if the product fails at a dilution lower than the MVD, the test may be repeated with a greater dilution, not exceeding the MVD.
questions.reference: USP <85> Gel-Clot Technique › Limit Test › Interpretation

questions.question: Which statement about incubation and reading in the gel-clot test is correct?

options.A: Typically incubate at 37 ± 1° for 60 ± 2 minutes, gently shaking the tubes during incubation to speed gel formation; a turbid solution is read as positive
options.B: Typically incubate at 30-35° for 14 days, observing the gel daily; any color change is read as positive
options.C: Typically incubate at 37 ± 1° for 60 ± 2 minutes avoiding vibration; after inversion through approximately 180°, the test is positive if a firm gel remains intact
options.D: Typically incubate at 25° for 24 hours and read absorbance with a spectrophotometer; a value above the threshold is read as positive

questions.explanation: Incubate for a fixed time according to the lysate manufacturer's instructions (typically 60 ± 2 minutes at 37 ± 1°), avoiding vibration; invert the tube through approximately 180° in one smooth motion, and if a firm gel has formed and remains in place the result is positive, while the absence of an intact gel is negative. Shaking the tubes, incubating for 14 days, and reading by absorbance are not how gel-clot is read.
questions.reference: USP <85> Gel-Clot Technique › Preparatory Testing › Test for Confirmation of Labeled Lysate Sensitivity (incubation and reading of gel integrity)

questions.topic: Standard curve criteria for photometric techniques
questions.question: Which requirement for establishing a standard curve in the turbidimetric or chromogenic technique is correct?

options.A: Perform it for each lot of lysate; use at least three concentrations, each in at least triplicate, with |r| of at least 0.980
options.B: Perform it once a year; use at least two concentrations, each in duplicate, with the absolute value of the correlation coefficient r of at least 0.900
options.C: Perform it for each lot of lysate; use at least five concentrations, each tested once, with the absolute value of the correlation coefficient r of at least 0.990
options.D: Perform it only when the analyst or instrument is changed; use at least three concentrations, each in duplicate, with no requirement for r

questions.explanation: Verification of the standard curve must be performed for each lot of lysate, using at least three endotoxin concentrations within the range given by the manufacturer, each in at least triplicate, and the absolute value of the correlation coefficient r must be greater than or equal to 0.980.
questions.reference: USP <85> Photometric Quantitative Techniques › Preparatory Testing › Assurance of Criteria for the Standard Curve

questions.question: How do the detection principles of the turbidimetric and chromogenic techniques differ?

options.A: Turbidimetric measures whether the gel is firm; chromogenic measures the integrity of the gel after the tube is inverted; both can use only the endpoint method
options.B: Turbidimetric can use only the endpoint method; chromogenic can use only the kinetic method; the two cannot be used interchangeably
options.C: Turbidimetric measures the increase in turbidity of the reaction mixture; chromogenic measures the chromophore released in the reaction; both have endpoint and kinetic methods
options.D: The principles are the same, with both measuring gel formation, and differ only in incubation temperature and the way readings are taken

questions.explanation: Turbidimetric is a photometric method that measures the rise in turbidity of the reaction mixture, whereas chromogenic measures the chromophore released from a chromogenic peptide after endotoxin reacts with the lysate. Both can be endpoint or kinetic methods, and the incubation temperature in both follows the lysate manufacturer's recommendation (usually 37 ± 1°). Reading a gel is the gel-clot approach.
questions.reference: USP <85> Photometric Quantitative Techniques › Turbidimetric Technique; Chromogenic Technique

questions.question: In the gel-clot inhibition/enhancement test, what are Solution B and Solution C, and how is it determined that the sample has no interfering factors?

options.A: B is water plus 2λ endotoxin; C is the sample without endotoxin; the sensitivity of B must be exactly the same as that of C for the sample to be free of interfering factors
options.B: B is the sample without endotoxin; C is water plus endotoxin; B must be positive and agree with the result of C for the sample to be free of interference
options.C: B and C are both sample solutions, tested at different dilutions; both must be negative for the sample to be free of interference
options.D: B is the sample plus a series of endotoxin concentrations starting at 2λ; C is Water for BET plus the same series; the sensitivity of B must be within 0.5λ-2λ

questions.explanation: Solution B adds a series of endotoxin concentrations starting at 2λ to the sample solution to test for interference; Solution C adds the same series to Water for BET and is used to confirm the lysate sensitivity. If the sensitivity determined for B is not less than 0.5λ and not more than 2λ, the sample contains no interfering factors under those conditions.
questions.reference: USP <85> Gel-Clot Technique › Preparatory Testing › Test for Interfering Factors, Table 1

questions.question: In a photometric interference test, after endotoxin is added to the sample and the endotoxin content of the sample itself is subtracted, the recovery is only about 30%. How should this be judged and handled?

options.A: The recovery is outside the 50%-200% range, so the sample contains interfering factors; repeat the test at a greater dilution, not exceeding the MVD
options.B: A low recovery only means the sample's own endotoxin content is very low and does not indicate interference; it may be considered compliant and released directly
options.C: The recovery is within the acceptable range, because it only has to be no more than 200%, and a low recovery needs no action
options.D: When recovery is insufficient, increase the amount of lysate and raise the dilution directly above the MVD before retesting, until the recovery meets the criterion

questions.explanation: In photometric methods, the measured concentration of the endotoxin added to the sample must be within 50%-200% of the known added amount for the sample to be considered free of interference; outside this range, interfering factors are present, and the test must be repeated at a greater dilution (not exceeding the MVD) or the interference must be removed by validated treatments such as filtration, neutralization, dialysis, or heating.
questions.reference: USP <85> Photometric Quantitative Techniques › Preparatory Testing › Test for Interfering Factors

questions.question: In the photometric interference test (Table 4), how are Solution B and Solution D designed?

options.A: B is the sample plus endotoxin at the midpoint concentration of the standard curve; D is a Water for BET negative control, whose value must not exceed the blank limit
options.B: B is Water for BET plus endotoxin at the lowest concentration; D is the sample solution without endotoxin, used to measure the sample's endotoxin background
options.C: B is the sample without endotoxin; D is the sample plus endotoxin at the midpoint concentration of the standard curve, used to calculate recovery
options.D: B and D are both Water for BET solutions, differing only in the number of replicates and the dilution factor

questions.explanation: Solution B is the sample at the same dilution as Solution A with endotoxin added at the midpoint (or near the midpoint) concentration of the standard curve; Solution D is the Water for BET negative control, and its result must not exceed the blank limit of the lysate or must be below the limit of detection for the test to be valid.
questions.reference: USP <85> Photometric Quantitative Techniques › Preparatory Testing › Test for Interfering Factors, Table 4

questions.question: According to the footnote in <85>, when verifying that a dry-heat procedure effectively removes endotoxin, what sensitivity of lysate should be used, and which chapter should be consulted?

options.A: A lysate with a sensitivity of not less than 1 EU/mL, referring to the relevant provisions of <71> Sterility Tests
options.B: A lysate of any sensitivity may be used, referring to the relevant provisions of <788> Particulate Matter
options.C: Lysate TS with a sensitivity of not less than 0.15 EU/mL, referring to Dry-Heat Sterilization in <1211>
options.D: A lysate with a sensitivity of not more than 0.15 EU/mL, referring to the provisions of <11> USP Reference Standards

questions.explanation: The footnote states that the validity of an endotoxin-removal procedure should be tested by referring to Dry-Heat Sterilization in <1211> Sterility Assurance, using Lysate TS with a sensitivity of not less than 0.15 EU/mL. <11> covers USP Reference Standards and is not relevant here.

questions.question: A sample interferes with the BET, and QC wants to eliminate the interference by filtration. What must be done to demonstrate that this treatment is effective?

options.A: It is sufficient that no endotoxin is detected in the treated sample; no separate recovery test is needed to show that the treatment is effective
options.B: Add standard endotoxin to the sample, apply the treatment, and test, confirming that the interference is eliminated and no endotoxin is lost
options.C: Add endotoxin to Water for BET and apply the treatment; the actual sample to be tested need not be used
options.D: Filtration is a recognized standard treatment, so its effectiveness for this product need not be separately demonstrated

questions.explanation: Interference can be overcome by suitable treatments such as filtration, neutralization, dialysis, or heating, but the treatment must be applied to the test sample spiked with standard endotoxin and then tested to show that it both eliminates the interference and does not cause a loss of endotoxin. The mere fact that no endotoxin is detected after treatment cannot rule out that the endotoxin was removed along with the interference.
questions.reference: USP <85> Gel-Clot Technique › Preparatory Testing › Test for Interfering Factors (treatment to overcome interference)
